transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I guess... I mean, the main thing is that I've just completely stopped caring about everything. Everything I used to actually look forward to. I manage construction sites for a living, right? It's a loud, high-stress job, dealing with contractors and deadlines all week, so I always used to really value my downtime. But lately... 

Take my fishing gear, for example. I spent all winter getting my tackle box organized, bought a new reel, the whole nine yards, getting ready for the spring. And it’s just sitting there. Untouched. Right out there in the garage. I walk past it every single morning on my way to the truck and I just feel... nothing. I don't even want to look at it, let alone pack it up and drive to the lake. 

And it's not just that, either. I have this woodshop out back. Usually, I'd be out there sanding something down, building cabinets, whatever, just to clear my head. Now, just the thought of walking out there and turning on the lathe... it feels like this massive, impossible chore. I can't bring myself to step foot in there. 

It's even happening with my family. My kids, they're great kids, they keep trying to get me to play chess with them in the evenings. We used to have this running tournament going on, keeping score on the fridge. And I sit down at the board with them now, because I know I'm supposed to, but I'm really just... I'm just going through the motions. I'm moving the pieces, but my head is empty. I'm not really there. I just don't care about any of it anymore, and I don't know how to fix it.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, it’s not like it happened overnight, you know? It’s not like I just woke up one Tuesday and decided I didn't care about fishing or the woodshop anymore. It kind of crept up on me. But if I really sit down and trace it back... I'd say it's been about a year and seven months. Yeah, a year and seven months, pretty much exactly. 

That was when... well, that was when my wife's health problems started. It just changed everything at home. Everything got turned upside down. Before that, we had our routine, you know? I'd come home from the site, we'd have dinner, I'd go out to the shop, she'd read or whatever. But then she got sick, and suddenly I was the one trying to hold it all together. The cooking, the cleaning, getting the kids to their things, on top of managing the crews at work, which is a 50-hour-a-week job on a good week. And at first, I was just running on adrenaline, just doing what needed to be done because you don't have a choice, right? You just put your head down and push through. But then the months started ticking by, and her health was still up and down, and the stress at home was just... it was like this heavy blanket over everything. 

And somewhere in all of that, maybe around the six-month mark of her being sick, I just started feeling... drained. Not just physically tired, but like... emotionally empty. Like someone pulled the plug and let all the water drain out of the tub. That's when I stopped going out to the shop. I told myself I was just too busy, too tired from taking care of everything else. But even when things stabilized a bit with her, even when I had a free Saturday afternoon, I just couldn't do it. And it's just been getting worse since then. So yeah, a year and seven months of this... whatever this is. It feels like a lifetime, honestly. I keep waiting to snap out of it, to wake up and feel like my old self again, but it just hasn't happened.
Have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, like fishing or working in your woodshop?

Yeah, exactly. Like I was mentioning just a minute ago about the garage and the shop, it's exactly that. I mean, it's not just that I don't have the time to do them anymore, it's that the actual feeling of wanting to do them is just... gone. Completely wiped out. 

Like with the woodshop, I used to love the smell of the sawdust, right? Pine, oak, walnut. I would spend hours just sourcing the right timber from this guy a couple towns over. I'd drive the truck down there on a Saturday morning, grab a coffee, talk to him about the grain, load up the bed... it was a whole ritual. And the fishing, too. It wasn't even about catching anything half the time. It was just being out on the water, away from the radios at the site, away from the framing contractors yelling at me about supply chain delays. It was my peace and quiet. 

And now I look at the lathe, or I look at the rods, and it's just dead weight. I don't get a single spark of joy from any of it. I actually tried to force it a couple weeks ago. I made myself go out to the shop because my wife kept telling me to go make something, saying it would make me feel better to get my hands dirty. So I went out there, turned on the overhead lights, and I just stood there for maybe twenty minutes staring at this half-finished birdhouse I started for my youngest daughter before everything went sideways with my wife's health. And I just... I couldn't even bring myself to pick up a piece of sandpaper. I just turned the lights back off, went back inside, and sat on the couch. 

It is like the part of my brain that actually enjoys things has just been completely shut off, and I don't know where the switch is to turn it back on. It's just so frustrating because those were the things that kept me sane, you know? And without them, I'm just empty.
Have you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, for a good part of the last two weeks?

Well... I mean, I guess it depends on what you mean by "down." But if you're asking if I've felt like this heavy, empty feeling most of the day, pretty much every day... then yeah. Definitely. It's not just the last two weeks, either, though the last two weeks have been particularly rough. 

It's like... I wake up at 5:00 AM, right? Because I have to be at the site early to make sure the materials were delivered right and the crews are actually showing up on time. And the second my alarm goes off, before my feet even hit the floor, this... this weight just settles on my chest. It's not even sadness, exactly. It's more like a complete lack of energy or hope or... anything. I just lie there in the dark, listening to my wife breathe, and I think about the entire day stretching out ahead of me, and it feels like I have to climb a mountain just to get out of bed and put my boots on. 

And then I get to the site, and normally I'd be energized by the noise, the progress, the problem-solving. But lately, I'm just sitting in the site trailer, staring at the blueprints, and I just feel so low. Like I'm at the bottom of a well. The foremen come in asking questions about the pouring schedule or the framing inspections, and I answer them, I do my job, but inside I'm just... dragging. Every hour feels like three hours. 

Then I come home, and like I said, I don't go to the shop, I don't touch the fishing gear. I just sit in my recliner. The kids are doing their homework, my wife is making dinner, and I'm physically in the room with them, but mentally I'm just sunk. It's this constant, low-level misery that just doesn't lift. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday morning or a Saturday afternoon. It's just always there, like a shadow I can't shake off. So yeah, nearly every day, most of the day... that's exactly what it is. It's exhausting, honestly. Just being awake feels exhausting.
Have you noticed a significant drop in your energy levels or felt unusually fatigued, even when you haven’t been doing much physically taxing?

Oh, God, yes. It’s exactly that. I mean, I know I just mentioned how heavy I feel when I wake up, but it doesn't get any better once I'm actually moving. It’s like... well, I’m a construction manager, right? So I’m used to being on my feet, walking the site, going up and down unfinished stairwells all day. I used to do it without even thinking, just bouncing around checking on the different trades. 

But now? By midmorning, like maybe ten or ten-thirty, I feel like I’ve already worked a full twelve-hour shift. And I haven't even done anything that physical! I'm mostly just looking at plans or talking to the subs. But when I actually have to go out and walk the project... man. Climbing the stairs with the crew used to be nothing, I'd take them two at a time, but now it literally feels like my body is carrying wet concrete. You know how dense and heavy wet concrete is? It’s like that's pumping through my legs instead of blood. 

Every single step up to the second or third floor is just this massive, monumental effort. I'll get to the top and I have to pretend I'm just stopping to inspect a joint or look at the HVAC routing, but really I'm just trying to catch my breath and keep my legs from giving out. And it's so frustrating because, like you said, I’m not the one swinging the hammer or hauling the drywall. I'm managing. I shouldn't be this wiped out. But I get back to the site trailer and I just collapse into my desk chair. I'll just sit there staring at my boots, feeling completely drained, dreading the next time my radio goes off and I have to stand back up. It’s this deep, bone-weary fatigue that just never goes away, no matter how little physical labor I actually do. It's like my battery is permanently stuck at one percent.
Have you been feeling like you’re a failure or that you’ve let people down, maybe even feeling guilty about things more than usual?

Yeah... yeah, that’s... that’s probably the worst part of all of this, honestly. It’s just this constant, loud loop playing in my head, telling me I’m failing everybody. 

I look at my wife—and I mentioned her health earlier, right? She’s dealing with all that, and I’m supposed to be her rock. I'm supposed to be the guy holding it all together for her and the kids, keeping the house running, being the strong one. But I’m just... I’m not. I look at them and I keep thinking I’ve completely failed my wife, I've failed my kids. I can’t even build a stupid birdhouse for my youngest daughter, you know? What kind of father can't even do that? 

And it doesn't stop at home, it bleeds right into work, too. The guys on the crew, the subs... they rely on me to keep the site running smoothly, to keep the project on schedule so they can feed their own families. But lately, if even the smallest thing goes sideways, I just completely spiral. Like, if there’s a cost overrun because the framing lumber spiked again, or if we get a safety issue flagged because some new kid didn't tie off on the scaffolding, or even if it's just me missing a routine vendor appointment because I was stuck in the trailer feeling sorry for myself... 

Normally, in the old days, I'd just fix it. That's my job, you solve the problem and move on. But now? I internalize every single piece of it. I take every little mistake or hiccup as this undeniable proof that I am just completely useless. I sit there and think, "See? You can't even manage a simple supply delivery, how are you supposed to manage a family?" 

It just gets so heavy. I get so wrapped up in this guilt that I actually start thinking... I mean, I really, truly believe it... that everyone would just be better off without me in charge. Like, if the company just brought in another project manager to run the site, things would run perfectly. And if my family just didn't have to deal with me dragging them down, being this miserable dead weight in the living room every night... they'd be happier. It’s just... I feel like everything I touch lately, I'm just ruining it, and I can't stop feeling so incredibly guilty for putting all these people through the burden of having to deal with me.
Have you ever felt so overwhelmed by these feelings that you've thought about hurting yourself or that life isn't worth living?

I... man, that’s a hard question to answer out loud. But... yeah. I guess I have. 

I told you earlier about how I wake up at 5:00 AM, right? Well, my commute to the site is about forty-five minutes. It’s mostly highway, and at that hour, it’s pitch black out. There’s almost nobody else on the road. Just me, the headlights, and the hum of the truck tires. I drive this big F-150, and usually, in the past, I’d use that time to listen to sports radio or run through the punch list for the day in my head, figuring out which subs need to be where. But lately... I don't even turn the radio on. I just drive in complete silence. 

And on those early drives, before anyone else is even awake, my mind just starts going to these really, really dark places. I’ll be sitting there, gripping the steering wheel, looking at the concrete dividers or the overpass pillars coming up in the headlights, and I catch myself thinking... you know, it would just be so much easier if I didn’t make it there. If I just didn't show up. Not just to work, but to... to anything. Just let it all stop. 

I'll be doing sixty-five, seventy miles an hour, and I look at the drop-off on the side of the interstate, and this thought just creeps in about just... turning the wheel. Just a quick jerk to the right. It wouldn’t even take much effort, just a flick of the wrist. And sometimes... honestly, doc, sometimes the thought of steering off the road scares the absolute hell out of me, because it feels too close. It doesn't feel like just a random, crazy thought that I can brush off. It feels like the barrier between me just thinking about it and my hands actually doing it is getting paper-thin. 

I think about my wife and the kids, and that whole loop of guilt I was just talking about, and it all just swirls together in the cab of that truck. I end up gripping the wheel so hard my knuckles go white just to keep myself in the center of the lane. I haven't... I haven't done anything, obviously. I'm sitting right here. But the fact that my brain even goes there, that it feels like a genuine, viable option to just end all this exhaustion... it’s terrifying. I never used to be a guy who thought like that. I build things for a living, you know? I don't destroy them. But in those mornings, in the dark, with the road just stretching out empty... it just feels like the only way to finally put the burden down.

doctor.question: Have you ever felt so overwhelmed by these feelings that you've thought about hurting yourself or that life isn't worth living?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: On those early drives before anyone else is awake, I catch myself thinking it would be easier if I just didn’t make it there, and sometimes the thought of steering off the road scares me because it feels too close.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have had thoughts about hurting myself or feeling that life isn't worth living, which directly corresponds to suicidal ideation and thoughts of death.

patient.answer:
I... man, that’s a hard question to answer out loud. But... yeah. I guess I have. 

I told you earlier about how I wake up at 5:00 AM, right? Well, my commute to the site is about forty-five minutes. It’s mostly highway, and at that hour, it’s pitch black out. There’s almost nobody else on the road. Just me, the headlights, and the hum of the truck tires. I drive this big F-150, and usually, in the past, I’d use that time to listen to sports radio or run through the punch list for the day in my head, figuring out which subs need to be where. But lately... I don't even turn the radio on. I just drive in complete silence. 

And on those early drives, before anyone else is even awake, my mind just starts going to these really, really dark places. I’ll be sitting there, gripping the steering wheel, looking at the concrete dividers or the overpass pillars coming up in the headlights, and I catch myself thinking... you know, it would just be so much easier if I didn’t make it there. If I just didn't show up. Not just to work, but to... to anything. Just let it all stop. 

I'll be doing sixty-five, seventy miles an hour, and I look at the drop-off on the side of the interstate, and this thought just creeps in about just... turning the wheel. Just a quick jerk to the right. It wouldn’t even take much effort, just a flick of the wrist. And sometimes... honestly, doc, sometimes the thought of steering off the road scares the absolute hell out of me, because it feels too close. It doesn't feel like just a random, crazy thought that I can brush off. It feels like the barrier between me just thinking about it and my hands actually doing it is getting paper-thin. 

I think about my wife and the kids, and that whole loop of guilt I was just talking about, and it all just swirls together in the cab of that truck. I end up gripping the wheel so hard my knuckles go white just to keep myself in the center of the lane. I haven't... I haven't done anything, obviously. I'm sitting right here. But the fact that my brain even goes there, that it feels like a genuine, viable option to just end all this exhaustion... it’s terrifying. I never used to be a guy who thought like that. I build things for a living, you know? I don't destroy them. But in those mornings, in the dark, with the road just stretching out empty... it just feels like the only way to finally put the burden down.

inference.note: The patient has endorsed suicidal ideation without a specific plan or intent, which suggests a more severe depressive episode (F32.3) or severe recurrent depressive episode (F33.3). This addition of suicidal ideation elevates the severity classification from moderate (F32.2/F33.2) to severe.
